raw_response:
I’m 64 this year, and I’ve worked these fields in Quzhou my whole life. I don’t make plans from a book, I make them from what I’ve seen on my own land. On my 16.9 mu, I’ll still keep the wheat-maize rotation as the main part because it is steady and keeps grain income coming, but I’ll leave part of the land in cotton because cotton spreads the risk. If grain price is only so-so, at least cotton can still bring some cash; if cotton has pests or the picking is troublesome, I still have wheat and maize. I have well water, so I’m not completely at the mercy of the sky, but pumping costs money, so I won’t water carelessly. Some people in my family work off-farm, so labor is not as free as before. Because of that, I won’t chase very high input. I’ll use a moderate rate, a little safer than cutting too much, because if fertilizer is too low and the crop turns weak, that loss hurts more than spending a bit extra.

For the wheat-maize land, I’ll keep about 10 mu in double cropping. Wheat I’ll sow in early October with a common improved local variety, not the most expensive seed. I usually put most fertilizer down as base, then add another bit at jointing if the stand looks yellow or weak. Wheat needs the water more reliably, so I’ll plan around three irrigations if the year is normal. After harvest in June, I’ll turn around fast and put in summer maize right away, because in our place that window is tight. I won’t do heavy tillage between wheat and maize, just quick residue clearing and rotary tillage or direct seeding if the machine can come on time. For cotton, I’ll keep 6.9 mu. Cotton can make money, but it ties up labor and needs more watching for insects, so I won’t expand it more at my age. I’ll use an improved cotton seed, put on moderate fertilizer, irrigate one or two times depending on rain, and spray only when I really see pressure.
